about: Albany Distilling Company was founded in 2011 by John Curtin and Matthew Jager, two teachers who hatched the idea over a pint at the Albany Pump Station. When the space next door came free, they opened Albany’s first licensed distillery since Prohibition, a short walk from the site of the Quackenbush Still House, the city’s first distillery, established in the mid-18th century. Jager left in 2014 to start his own distillery; Curtin now runs the company with co-owner Rick Sicari.

Ironweed takes its name from William Kennedy’s Pulitzer Prize-winning novel, set in Depression-era Albany. The bourbon is made from New York grain, 60% corn, 25% rye and 15% malted barley, milled on site, then mashed, fermented and distilled by the company itself. The new spirit comes off a column still and rests in new charred American white oak for at least two years; recent releases are reported at around four. Nothing is added but water, to bring it to 43%, or 86 proof.

Ironweed is the line that carried Albany Distilling beyond farmers’ markets and its own tasting room: the Ironweed Rye won gold from the American Craft Spirits Association in 2014, and the bourbon, rye and straight malt now share the label. Production has since moved to a building on Third Street roughly eight times the size of the original, with the bar and bottle shop downtown on Livingston Avenue.
